dataset.what_one_row_represents: songs.csv: one Billboard Hot 100 charting song with a male vocal lead, 1958-2019, with its Pandora register score (1-10), chart points, and peak rank. 2019.csv: one of 248 Hot 100 songs from 2019 (all genders) with register, gender, genre and a 0-10 'spoken' score. avg.csv: yearly mean register across the male-led songs. avg_top.csv: yearly mean register restricted to top-10 male-led songs.

ana_01.label: 2019 top-10 register hit a 60-year high (7.60)
ana_01.content: Among the male-led songs that reached the Billboard Hot 100's top 10 in 2019, the average Pandora register was 7.60 — the highest single-year value in the entire 60-year series. The previous record was 1988, the height of the hair-metal era, at 7.21. Every other year in the dataset sits below 7.21. The 2019 figure rests on only five top-10 male-led songs (Sucker, I Don't Care, If I Can't Have You, Talk, No Guidance), so it is technically a small sample — but four of the five score 7 or higher and two score 9, which is enough to lift the mean above any 1980s hair-metal year.

data_table.description: Yearly average register among top-10 male-led Hot 100 songs, 1958-2019

notable_instance.name: Khalid — 'Talk' (2019)
notable_instance.value: register 7 in a top-10 average of 7.6
notable_instance.why: One of the four high-register top-10 hits driving 2019 to its all-time top-10 record.

ana_02.label: All-songs register peaked in 1990 (7.08), not 2019
ana_02.content: The picture flips when you include every charting male-led Hot 100 song instead of just the top 10. By that measure, the late-1980s/early-1990s hair-metal years are the unambiguous peak: 1990 averages 7.08 — the highest in the series — followed by 1987 (7.08), 1988 (7.08), 1989 (7.04), and 1984 (7.04). 2019, in contrast, averages only 5.95 across all 80 male-led charting songs. That is below 1958. The headline is not that men today sing higher than they used to. It is that the songs that *win* now sing higher.

data_table.description: Yearly average register, all male-led Hot 100 songs, 1958-2019

ana_03.label: The 2019 top/all gap (1.65) is the largest in 60 years
ana_03.content: In a typical year, the average register of the top-10 male-led songs sits around 0.3-0.5 points above the average for all male-led charting songs. In 2019, that gap explodes to 1.65 — top-10 at 7.60 minus all-songs at 5.95. This is more than double the next-largest gap on record (0.78 in 2015) and a complete inversion of 1995, the only year where top-10 actually averaged below the all-songs mean (a gap of -0.25). Translation: in 2019, hitting the top 10 with a male voice required singing higher than almost any other path to the chart.

ana_04.label: The 2019 top-10 male-led songs
ana_04.content: The five 2019 top-10 male-led Hot 100 hits are: 'Sucker' by the Jonas Brothers (register 9, peaked #1), 'I Don't Care' by Ed Sheeran & Justin Bieber (register 5, #2), 'If I Can't Have You' by Shawn Mendes (register 9, #2), 'Talk' by Khalid (register 7, #3), and 'No Guidance' by Chris Brown ft. Drake (register 8, #9). Four of the five score 7 or higher; two score 9. The mean register of this set is 7.60. The single low-register exception, 'I Don't Care', is the only song that doesn't fit the pattern.

ana_05.label: Decade-by-decade picture: a U-shape with a 2019 spike
ana_05.content: Aggregated by decade, the average male-led Hot 100 register climbs from 5.77 in the late 1950s, rises through the 1960s (6.13) and 1970s (6.62), peaks in the 1980s (6.92), drifts back down through the 1990s (6.53), 2000s (6.08), and 2010s (6.06). The all-songs series tells a U-shaped story with the 1980s as the bell of the bell. The top-10 series follows the same shape — except the 2010s rebound at the very end, lifted entirely by 2019.

data_table.description: Decade-mean register, all-songs and top-10 series

ana_06.label: What a register score means: anchors at 2 and 10
ana_06.content: The Pandora 1-10 axis is anchored on the low end by songs like Isaac Hayes's 'Theme From Shaft' (register 2, #1 in 1971) and War's 'Low Rider' (register 2, #7 in 1975) — deep chest-voice or spoken-low deliveries. On the high end, register 10 covers 157 songs across 42 years. Famous 10s in the dataset include 'Sherry' by The Four Seasons (#1, 1962), 'Good Vibrations' by The Beach Boys (#1, 1966), 'I Want You Back' by The Jackson 5 (#1, 1969), Aerosmith's 'Dream On' (1973), Led Zeppelin's 'Immigrant Song' (1970), and Paul McCartney's 'Live And Let Die' (#2, 1973). The score collapses falsetto and high belt onto a single perceived-pitch axis.

ana_07.label: Full register distribution across 11,944 songs
ana_07.content: The full distribution of register values across all 11,944 male-led Hot 100 songs from 1958-2019 is single-peaked at 7 (27.7%, 3,310 songs), with 6 (21.4%) and 5 (19.7%) close behind. Only 0.2% of songs (29) score a 2 and only 1.3% (157) score a 10. The most extreme registers are rare — register-9-or-10 covers just 5.0% of the dataset. The bulk of male pop sits at registers 5, 6, 7 — middle-to-moderately-high, what most listeners would call a comfortable tenor.

data_table.description: Frequency of each register score across the full songs.csv (1958-2019)

ana_08.label: 1980s share of high-register songs (>=8): 30-40%
ana_08.content: The 1980s' high-register dominance shows up at the song level too. From 1979 through 1991, the share of charting male-led songs with register 8 or higher sits in a 31-40% band every single year — peaking at 40.2% in 1988. By contrast, in 2017 only 5.8% of charting male-led songs scored 8 or higher (the lowest in the dataset), and 2019 had 16.2%. The 1980s peak was a high-register monoculture in a way 2019 is not.

data_table.description: Share of charting male-led songs with register>=8, by year, 1958-2019

ana_09.label: Genre split in 2019: rap pulls register down, ballads push it up
ana_09.content: Inside 2019.csv, the genre split is stark. Rap/Hip hop's 108 charting songs average register 4.45 — the lowest of any major genre. R&B (3 songs) averages 7.33. The large 'no genre' bucket (the bucket Pandora uses for songs that don't fit a single label, often pop/dance/electronic crossovers) averages 6.36 and contains nearly all of 2019's high-register songs (24 of the 27 with register>=8). Country averages 5.30, Pop 6.00. The same pattern shows up in the 'spoken' axis: songs that score 0 on the spoken (i.e., fully sung) average 6.31 in register; songs that score 8-10 (rapped) average 4.14.

ana_10.label: Female-led songs in 2019 average higher than male-led (6.51 vs 5.12)
ana_10.content: Among 2019 Hot 100 songs, female-led tracks (n=61) average a register of 6.51 — far above male-led (n=182, mean 5.12) and duets (n=5, mean 5.60). On the surface this is unsurprising: women generally sing higher than men. But the gap matters because it sets a baseline: the 2019 male top-10 average of 7.60 lifts male voices above the year's female average — a stylistic crossover that is genuinely unusual at the very top of the chart.

ana_11.label: 1990 was the all-time all-songs register peak (7.08)
ana_11.content: Sorted by all-songs mean register, the dataset's top decade by far is 1979-1991 — twelve consecutive years of mean register at 6.86 or higher. 1990 (7.0807) edges out 1987 (7.0802) and 1988 (7.0782) for the all-time peak. By 1992 the average drops to 6.48 and never recovers past 6.40 again. This is the unambiguous baseline against which the modern top-10 spike must be read.

data_table.description: Top 10 years by all-songs mean register

ana_12.label: 2017 was the lowest-register year in the dataset
ana_12.content: On the all-songs series, 2017 averaged 5.7226 — the lowest single-year value across the entire 1958-2019 window, undercutting even 1959 (5.7442). This is the year of the post-Drake mumble-rap surge, when much of the male-led Hot 100 was rapped at low pitch. Two years later, 2019's top-10 spiked to an all-time high while the all-songs average barely climbed. The shape of pop changed at the top, not at the base.

ana_13.label: Register-10 songs are concentrated in 1962-1992
ana_13.content: Of the 157 register-10 songs in the dataset, 96% land between 1962 and 1992. After 1997 there are only 10 register-10 songs in the next 22 years combined; 2019 has zero. Yet the 2019 top-10 average can still hit 7.60 because the modern male-led top-10 leans on registers 7-9 rather than 10. The performances that win the chart now are very high — but not stratospherically high.

caveats.content: songs.csv is restricted to male-led Hot 100 songs. The Pudding's article focuses on male voice trends; female and duet artists appear only in 2019.csv as a comparison point. Gender labelling matches Pandora's editorial coding.

2019 is unusual in songs.csv: only 80 male-led entries appear (vs 129 in 2018, 343 in 1966). The Pudding article notes this reflects the rise of solo-rap dominance — many 2019 chart entries were dropped from the male-singing analysis because their primary delivery was rapped, not sung. Top-10 averages built on 5 songs are statistically thinner than top-10 averages from 1966 (where 73 male-led top-10s charted).

Pandora register is hand-coded by musicologists on a 1-10 ordinal scale. It collapses chest voice and falsetto onto a single perceived-pitch axis, so a register=9 song could be belted in chest voice or sung in falsetto. The dataset cannot tell those apart.

2019.csv labels 1 song as 'female' twice (the same row appears with 'no genre' and the duplicate 'no genreno genre' label). After cleaning the duplicate-label rows fold into 'no genre'. Genre rows for 2019 are sparse: 'no genre' (112) and 'Rap/Hip hop' (108) account for 88% of 2019 entries.
